storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the objection as a person pushing back across a table, not as an abstract rule.
storyboard.claim: A listener objects to capping savings in today's world.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman leaning forward across a cafe table, challenging the savings cap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After annuity products for longevity risk: the counter-argument arrives.

storyboard.addedInformation: Names the billionaires-and-biotech fantasy as the specific objection to answer.
storyboard.claim: What if biotech massively extends life and the money is gone?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Narrator listing the longevity moonshots — stem cells, nanobots — on a modern office screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the objection: the reason capping savings feels dangerous.

storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the fantasy outcome directly: a vigorous 90-year-old, the best case the objection imagines.
storyboard.claim: The fantasy: reaching 90 spry and needing cash.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ann, fit and energetic, mid-stride in workout gear — the spry-90 dream.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Narrows the longevity what-if to a single vivid person.

storyboard.addedInformation: The empty wallet says the fear plainly: spent at 50, broke for the Mars trip.
storyboard.claim: Fear of spending at 50 and needing the money later for something huge.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman holding open an empty wallet, staring at a travel poster of a Mars colony.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The what-if gets its price tag: a Mars trip with no money left.

storyboard.addedInformation: Puts Perkins on screen as the blunt answerer before his quote lands.
storyboard.claim: Perkins answers with blunt statistical reality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill Perkins at his desk, about to deliver the grounded rebuttal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the fantasy to the man who demolishes it.

storyboard.addedInformation: The pointing finger prices the trade: guaranteed 30s–50s versus a sci-fi 90s.
storyboard.claim: Don't sacrifice guaranteed prime decades for a sci-fi old age.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Perkins pointing at a timeline of a life, tapping the 30s–50s band while Everyman watches.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Perkins's question: what you would trade away for the longevity bet.

storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the real probable outcome — a hospital bed, not a nanobot miracle — against the hope.
storyboard.claim: The likely reality is a ventilator, not a nanobot cure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman slumped in a sterile hospital bed, eyes on a small poster of a miracle cure.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the trade to its probable payoff: the ventilator, not Mars.

storyboard.addedInformation: The cemetery hill makes the mic drop literal: bet prime years on a sliver of probability and this is where it ends.
storyboard.claim: Sacrificing prime years for a tiny probability ends at the grave.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Perkins gesturing toward gravestones on a dusk cemetery hill.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The mic drop after the ventilator: Perkins names the destination.

storyboard.addedInformation: The wallet opens toward experience: money leaving the hand becomes a beach memory.
storyboard.claim: Stop paying the fear tax; turn money into memory now.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman on a bright beach, holding his wallet open toward the waves — spending it on the moment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the grave warning to the prescription: spend before the window closes.

storyboard.addedInformation: The family icon names the interrupting voice every listener hears: the kids.
storyboard.claim: The audience's loudest objection: what about the kids?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman at home with the family icon glowing beside him — children in the doorway.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from spending on yourself to the scream from the steering wheels.

storyboard.addedInformation: The clutched wallet plus the will-and-estate icon expose the defense as hoarding, not generosity.
storyboard.claim: Hoarding is justified as leaving money for kids or charity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman clutching his wallet to his chest beside estate papers — saving 'for them'.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the knee-jerk defense behind the kids objection.

storyboard.addedInformation: The strike style rejects the whole method: dying-to-give is crossed out, not debated.
storyboard.claim: Waiting until death to give is objectively terrible timing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A struck will beside a sealed inheritance: timing that kills generosity.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The hosts turn on the defense: the timing itself is the crime.

storyboard.addedInformation: The late-arriving check in an older woman's hand shows a refund, not a rescue.
storyboard.claim: An inheritance at 60 refunds a life already lived.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Elizabeth, late 60s, holding a large check that arrived decades too late.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The core insight: why a 60-year-old's inheritance changes nothing.

storyboard.addedInformation: weak: sorts the will-method's three unknowns into visible buckets the narration only lists.
storyboard.claim: A will gives random amounts at a random time to random people.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three buckets filling unpredictably: amounts, timing, heirs — the three Rs of wills.
storyboard.onScreenText: RANDOM AMOUNTS / RANDOM TIMING / RANDOM HEIRS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Structures the refund problem: the three randomnesses of dying-to-give.

storyboard.addedInformation: Her worried study of a family photo makes the unknown-heir problem personal.
storyboard.claim: You don't know what will be left or who will be alive to get it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Elizabeth studying a family photo, doing the grim math of care costs and surviving heirs.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Unpacks the sorter: the unknowns of care costs and surviving heirs.

storyboard.addedInformation: The stiff climb up the stairs shows the body's expiry date better than any chart.
storyboard.claim: At 62 the body is already failing as the kids leave home.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Elizabeth wincing up suburban porch stairs, knees popping, past a quiet empty-nest street.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks the listener to inhabit the 62-year-old heir: imagine this.

storyboard.addedInformation: The big check lands in a life that no longer needs it — nice gesture, dead timing.
storyboard.claim: A $250,000 estate check arrives when it is barely needed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Elizabeth holding a $250,000 estate check in her living room, more puzzled than joyful.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The hypothetical inheritance lands in her hands.

storyboard.addedInformation: The paid-off house around her proves the money's peak use expired years earlier.
storyboard.claim: The mortgage is paid, the hard years survived, the trip now impossible.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Elizabeth sitting in her paid-off living room, a faded backpacking poster from age 25 on the wall.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deflates the $250,000: every battle it could have won is already over.

storyboard.addedInformation: A money curve and a body curve visibly separating on a chart stages decoupling.
storyboard.claim: The money arrives decoupled from its maximum utility.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Narrator beside a chart where the money curve and the body's ability curve drift apart.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the tragedy behind the backpacking poster: maximum utility missed.

storyboard.addedInformation: The highlighted window on the life timeline gives savers the exact years to aim at.
storyboard.claim: The optimal giving window is ages 26 to 35.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Narrator pointing at a glowing 26–35 window on a life timeline.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the tragedy to the prescription: when the money should move.

storyboard.addedInformation: The house key in a young buyer's hand shows exactly what the money buys: the front door.
storyboard.claim: At the sweet spot the money buys a first home amid crushing rent.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman holding up new house keys before a modest first home on a suburban street.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First proof of the window: the down payment that beats the rent trap.

storyboard.addedInformation: The shield plus the briefcase show the mechanism: protection that makes risk possible.
storyboard.claim: Early money funds business risks and buys sleep during hard years.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman with a briefcase, a protective shield glowing behind him as he pitches a business.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second and third proof: the risk fund and the anxiety relief.

storyboard.addedInformation: Four empty chairs around her kitchen table count the kids she raised alone.
storyboard.claim: Virginia raised four kids, mostly as a struggling single mother.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Virginia alone at a worn kitchen table, surrounded by signs of four raised children.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the principle to its human proof: Virginia's story begins.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slumped shoulders over unpaid bills show decades of bleeding-edge stress in one posture.
storyboard.claim: She lived for decades at the bleeding edge of poverty.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Virginia slumped over a pile of bills under harsh kitchen light, keeping the lights on.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The depth of her struggle: stressed out of her mind for decades.

storyboard.addedInformation: The will-and-estate icon plus the check at 49 make the delay the visible villain.
storyboard.claim: At 49 her mother's death finally brought her $130,000.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Virginia, 49, holding her mother's $130,000 bequest letter — relief mixed with grief.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The inheritance finally arrives — nineteen years too late.

storyboard.addedInformation: Her flat stare to camera carries the book's verbatim verdict: at 30 there would have been no scramble.
storyboard.claim: Money received at 30 compounds a life; late inheritance cannot.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A young adult catching a gift of money at 30: the transfer landing when it compounds.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Virginia's own verdict: the money existed all along and still missed her.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slump beside the untouched gift shows good intentions with destroyed value.
storyboard.claim: Good intentions, but the timing destroyed the money's value.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Virginia slumped beside a wrapped gift delivered after the struggle ended.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The moral of Virginia: intention was good, timing was fatal.

storyboard.addedInformation: Pivots the lens from family to charity with Sylvia Bloom's name on the desk file.
storyboard.claim: Charitable giving suffers the exact same delay inefficiency.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman handing a gift to charity while its value leaks away: the same inefficiency.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends Virginia's lesson from kids to charity: tell me about Sylvia Bloom.

storyboard.addedInformation: The coin pile beside a subway token contrasts frugal decades with the unspent millions.
storyboard.claim: A frugal secretary died at 96 with $8 million for charities.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A subway token beside a towering stack of coins: Sylvia Bloom's frugal life and $8 million bequest.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sylvia Bloom's facts: subway every day, $8 million at death.

storyboard.addedInformation: The thoughtful pause concedes the beauty before the economics demolish it.
storyboard.claim: Beautiful on paper — but the temporal economics fail.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Narrator pausing thoughtfully over the $8 million charity announcement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concedes the gesture's beauty before questioning its timing.

storyboard.addedInformation: The compounding-goodwill curve on screen shows decades of lost scholarships in one gap.
storyboard.claim: The charities needed the money 30 years earlier; early gifts compound.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host presenting a gift to a young recipient: funded in 1990, not 2020.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The temporal economics: a 1990 scholarship beats a 2020 lump sum.

storyboard.addedInformation: A young man's worried face beside the giant check stages the fear: will this ruin him?
storyboard.claim: Won't a big check at 26 breed spoiled trust-fund monsters?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jason, mid-20s, staring at an oversized check — ambition visibly draining away.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pushback: handing a 26-year-old a fortune sounds like ruin.

storyboard.addedInformation: His thoughtful look weighs the folk theory the narration voices: is struggle the teacher?
storyboard.claim: Isn't the struggle itself what builds character?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jason thinking hard, backpack on — the struggling young man as character argument.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sharpens the pushback: struggle as character-building.

storyboard.addedInformation: The strike rejects the straw man: nobody prescribed a blank check.
storyboard.claim: The concern assumes a lump sum — but transfer need not be one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Narrator crossing out a giant blank check — the rejected straw man.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the monsters fear: it assumes a blank check nobody proposed.

storyboard.addedInformation: The trust documents in his hands show structured help: loans paid, no blank check.
storyboard.claim: Structure it: trusts, student loans, a targeted down payment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jason happily holding structured trust papers — student-loan payoff, not a blank check.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The alternative: targeted, structured transfers instead of a windfall.

storyboard.addedInformation: The strike crosses out 'generous' over a coffin: dying-to-give is the opposite of generosity.
storyboard.claim: Waiting until death to transfer wealth is not generosity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Narrator before gravestones beside a coffin: dying-to-give fails the definition of generosity.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The philosophical turn: die-to-give fails the definition of generosity.

storyboard.addedInformation: The cemetery tableau states the blunt legal fact: a corpse holds nothing; the state moves the pile.
storyboard.claim: You are just dead; the legal system moves assets a corpse can't hold.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Narrator gesturing at a fresh grave where legal papers, not a person, transfer the estate.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The blunt mechanism: death transfers assets by law, not by love.

storyboard.addedInformation: The gift changing hands between living people shows agency: generosity requires being alive.
storyboard.claim: Generosity requires agency — give it when it matters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Everyman joyfully handing a wrapped gift to living hands — giving while it counts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the corpse to the cure: living hands giving to living hands.

storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's turn-to-camera bridges wealth transfer to the foundation beneath it all.
storyboard.claim: Beneath spending and giving lies the ultimate currency.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Narrator turning to camera as money imagery drains away — something deeper remains.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridge beat: when and who are settled; now the currency behind both.

storyboard.addedInformation: Her vigorous celebration on the beach prices every dollar: health sets what money can buy. (No wallet icon: 'health is the wallet' is a metaphor that would read as literal money.)
storyboard.claim: Healthspan is the wallet; health is the exchange rate of joy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ann celebrating mid-motion on a bright beach — the healthy body that makes dollars joyful.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The foundation lands: none of the timing matters without the body to spend it.
